subhead: Take a free practice quiz or point your phone at any Intro Psych exam question for an instant, explained answer — decode the terminology, not just memorize it, without the guesswork.
metaTitle: Introductory Psychology Practice Quiz & Questions | Cambo
metaDescription: Free Introductory Psychology quiz and practice questions with instant, explained answers. Research methods, cognition, developmental psychology, social psychology, and abnormal psych basics.
whyItWorks: Intro Psych exams love near-identical terms that mean very different things — classical vs. operant conditioning, reliability vs. validity, correlation vs. causation — and the trick question is usually about telling two similar concepts apart. Cambo reads the exact question and explains which concept actually applies and why the others don't fit.

sampleQuestions.q: A researcher finds that ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in the summer. What does this best illustrate?
options: Ice cream sales cause drowning deaths
Correlation does not imply causation — a third variable (warm weather) likely explains both
Drowning deaths cause an increase in ice cream sales
The two variables are unrelated and the pattern is coincidental noise
sampleQuestions.a: Correlation does not imply causation — both variables likely rise because of a confounding third variable, warm weather, which increases both swimming and ice cream consumption.

sampleQuestions.q: In Pavlov's classic experiment, a dog begins salivating at the sound of a bell that was repeatedly paired with food. What type of learning does this demonstrate?
sampleQuestions.a: Classical conditioning — a previously neutral stimulus (the bell) comes to trigger a response (salivation) after being repeatedly paired with a stimulus (food) that already triggered it.

sampleQuestions.q: A child believes that a tall, narrow glass holds more liquid than a short, wide glass, even after watching the same amount of water poured between them. According to Piaget, this child has not yet developed which ability?
sampleQuestions.a: Conservation — the understanding that a quantity stays the same despite changes in its shape or appearance, typically developed during Piaget's concrete operational stage.

sampleQuestions.q: A personality test gives a person very different scores each time they take it, even though their personality hasn't changed. What is this test lacking?
sampleQuestions.a: Reliability — the consistency of a measure. A test can be reliable without being valid, but inconsistent results across repeated administrations point to a reliability problem specifically.

sampleQuestions.q: In a study on obedience, participants were told by an authority figure to administer what they believed were increasingly painful shocks to another person. This describes which classic study?
sampleQuestions.a: Milgram's obedience study — it demonstrated that a striking majority of ordinary participants would follow an authority figure's instructions to inflict apparent harm on a stranger.

sampleQuestions.q: Which of the following best describes the medical model of abnormal psychology?
options: Psychological disorders are viewed as illnesses with underlying biological causes that can be diagnosed and treated
Psychological disorders result entirely from learned behaviors and can be unlearned through conditioning
Psychological disorders are defined purely by how far a person's behavior deviates from social norms
Psychological disorders are best explained by unconscious childhood conflicts alone
sampleQuestions.a: The medical model treats psychological disorders as illnesses with identifiable biological or physiological causes, diagnosable through symptoms and treatable — similar to how physical illness is approached.

faqs.q: What topics does Intro to Psychology usually cover?
faqs.a: Most intro courses cover research methods and statistics, biological psychology, sensation and perception, learning, memory and cognition, developmental psychology, personality, social psychology, and an overview of psychological disorders and treatment.

faqs.q: Is Intro Psychology usually a lab science or a gen-ed elective?
faqs.a: It's typically a 3-credit-hour social/behavioral science gen-ed, though some schools offer a companion 1-credit lab section that fulfills a separate lab-science requirement.

It depends heavily on the instructor and section size, but large-lecture intro courses commonly curve exams, especially multiple-choice midterms, since raw score distributions can vary a lot between test versions.

faqs.q: What's the difference between clinical psychology and the general psychology covered in this course?
faqs.a: Intro Psychology surveys the whole field at a broad level — biological, cognitive, developmental, and social psychology included. Clinical psychology is a specific subfield focused on diagnosing and treating mental health disorders, usually studied in depth only in upper-level or graduate coursework.

faqs.q: Do I need a math or science prerequisite for Intro Psychology?
faqs.a: Generally no — it's usually an entry-level course with no prerequisites, though the research-methods and statistics unit does involve some basic quantitative reasoning.
